pos: noun or participle which takes the aux. verb suru
headline: “Peace of mind” is an old Chinese compound, and the same spelling has a twin reading with rendaku.

sources.quote: From Middle Chinese compound 安心 (MC 'an sim). Compare modern Chinese 安心 (ānxīn).

headline: Soap is, in Chinese, “stone lye”.

sources.quote: Appears to be from Middle Chinese 石鹼 (MC dzyek keamX, literally “stone + lye; soap”).

headline: A men's suit may be tied to English “civil clothes”, Savile Row or Cheviot — and the kanji say “wide back”.

sources.quote: Unknown, but thought to be related to English civil clothes, Savile Row, or Cheviot.
The kanji are ateji (当(あ)て字(じ)); they literally mean "back" + "wide" ("wide-backed").

headline: A balloon is a “wind ship”, and the word seems to have been coined in Japan around 1860.

sources.quote: Appears to be a coinage in Japanese from Middle Chinese-derived roots, as a compound of 風 (fū, “wind”) + 船 (sen, “ship, boat, vessel”).
First cited to a text from 1860.

meaning: indeed, truly, as one would expect
headline: さすが is “sasuga ni” with its last syllable dropped, and the reason for its kanji is still an open question.

sources.quote: From さすがに (sasuga ni) with omission of the final に (ni). The standalone term without the final に (ni) is first cited to the late 800s.
The kanji are jukujikun (熟(じゅく)字(じ)訓(くん)).

headline: “Fool” is spelled “horse + deer”, but those characters were fitted to the sound — probably an allusion to an old Chinese saying.

sources.quote: Probably originally a transcription of Sanskrit मोह (moha, “folly”), used as a cant term among monks. However, Sanskrit पाक (pāka, “naïve, foolish”) is more similar phonetically and grammatically.

Alternatively, may have arisen from the same root as Old Japanese 痴 (woko, modern oko, “stupidity, ridiculousness”). However, this theory is problematic phonologically, as the /b/ ↔ /w/ shift is difficult to explain.

The characters 馬鹿 (literally “horse + deer”) are ateji (当(あ)て字(じ)), probably chosen as an allusion to Literary Chinese 指鹿為馬 (“to deliberately misinterpret and invert right and wrong”, literally “to point to a deer and call it a horse”) (see that entry for more).

pos: noun or participle which takes the aux. verb suru
headline: “Shortage” is, in Chinese, just “not enough”.

sources.quote: From Middle Chinese 不足 (MC pjuw tsjowk, “not + enough”).

headline: Midnight is the “middle of the night”.

sources.quote: Compound of 夜(よ) (yo, “night”) + 中(なか) (naka, “middle”).

headline: “Regrettable” is “lingering” plus “concern”, and appears in texts from the late 1500s.

sources.quote: Seems to be a Japanese coinage from Middle Chinese-derived roots, as a compound of 残 (zan, “remaining, lingering”) + 念 (nen, “concern”). Appears in texts from the late 1500s.

headline: The chair began as a seat for court officials and came to mean the wooden seat of a Zen priest.

sources.quote: /isi/ → /isɨ/ → /isu/

Originally 倚子 (ishi), referring to seats with or without rests used by higher court officials. With the arrival of Zen Buddhism to Japan, possibly a later borrowing from Middle Chinese 椅子 (MC 'jeX tsiX) or directly from Mandarin 椅子 (yǐzi, literally "chair" + diminutive suffix), the meaning shifted to wooden seats used by priests.

headline: Katakana is “partial kana” — the same 片 as in 方, “direction”.

sources.quote: Compound of 片 (kata, “part”) + 仮名 (kana). 片 is in turn a cognate with 方 (kata).

meaning: high and low, up and down
headline: “Up and down” came over from Chinese as a ready-made compound — and じょうげ is likely its first reading.

sources.quote: /d͡ʑauɡe/ → /d͡ʑɔːɡe/ → /d͡ʑoːɡe/
From Middle Chinese compound 上下 (dzyangᴴ hæ^X, literally “up and down”). Compare modern Cantonese reading soeng⁶ haa⁶, Hakka song-ha, or Min Nan alternative reading chiūⁿ hā.
The goon reading, so likely the initial borrowing.

headline: Noisy is “making noise” plus an adjective-making ending.

sources.quote: From the 未然形 (mizenkei, irrealis stem) of 騒ぐ (sawagu, “to make noise”) + しい (shii, “adjectivizing suffix”).

headline: A porter is a clipped “bellboy”, while a boy is just an English boy.

sources.quote: Borrowed from English boy.
Clipping of ベルボーイ (berubōi), borrowed from English bellboy.

headline: “Proactive” is the “positive pole” with an adjective-forming suffix.

morphemes.meaning: positive procession towards an objective; the positive pole

sources.quote: Compound of 積極(せっきょく) (sekkyoku, “positive procession towards an objective; the positive pole”) + 的(てき) (-teki, adjective-forming suffix).

headline: “Trouble” is spelled with kanji that are only ateji — so where the word came from is an open question.

sources.quote: The kanji are ateji (当(あ)て字(じ)).

headline: “The world” began as a translation of a Sanskrit term for “region or part of the world”.

sources.quote: From Middle Chinese 世界 (MC syejH keajH), originally a translation of Sanskrit लोकधातु (lokadhātu, “region or part of the world”). Compare Hokkien 世界 (sè-kài).

headline: A birthday is a “birth day”, with ひ voiced to び.

sources.quote: Compound of 誕生(たんじょう) (tanjō, “birth”) + 日(び) (-bi, “day”).
The hi reading for 日 changes to bi as an instance of rendaku (連濁).

meaning: to be different; to differ; wrong
headline: “To differ” began as “roads that cross” — dated to 974.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese. Compound of 道 (chi, “road, way”) + 交う (kau, “cross, exchange”). The kau changes to gau as an instance of rendaku (連濁).
First cited to the Kagerō Nikki of 974, and likely extant earlier given the initial citing in 965 of derived form 違える (chigaeru, “to keep something from happening”)
Similar, but not related, to tagau reading.

headline: A volcano's crater is a “fire mouth” — and the same two characters have more than one reading.

sources.quote: Compound of 火 (ka, “fire”) + 口 (kō, “hole”).

headline: Furigana are kana you “assign” to a character; the word dates from 1813.

sources.quote: From 振(ふ)り (furi, “assigning”, 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 振(ふ)る (furu, “to assign, to stick on, to apportion”)) + 仮名(かな) (kana, “kana”).
The kana changes to gana as an instance of rendaku (連濁).
First attested in 1813.

pos: noun or participle which takes the aux. verb suru
headline: Massage reached Japanese through English and French, and began in an Arabic word for “feel, touch”.

sources.quote: From English massage, from French massage, from masser (“to massage”), borrowed around the end of the 18th century from Arabic مَسَّ (massa, “feel, touch”) + French -age.

headline: Fabric or dough is “raw ground” — and the word first meant bare, unlacquered wood.

sources.quote: ⟨kidi⟩ → /kiʑi/
Compound of 生 (ki, “crude, pure, raw”) + 地 (ji, “earth; skin”).
Originally written 木地, a transparent compound of 木 (ki, “wood”) + 地 (di, “earth; skin”), referring to the bare wooden surface of an object before lacquer or paint was applied.
Attested from at least the medieval period in this sense. (First cited in Vocabulario da Lingoa de Iapam)

pos: noun or participle which takes the aux. verb suru
headline: ひとこと is the native reading; the same spelling also has Chinese-derived readings, one likely borrowed first.

sources.quote: Compound of 一(ひと) (hito, “one”) + 言(こと) (koto, “word, speech”).

headline: The month after next can be broken down two ways, and references disagree on which is right.

sources.quote: Analyzed by references as either a compound of 再来 (sarai, “two next, the one after next”) + 月 (getsu, “month”), or as a compound of 再 (sa, “again, one more”) + 来月 (raigetsu, “next month”).
First attested in 1799.

headline: “Healthy” began as the fundamental force of the cosmos, until it was confused with a word for recovery.

sources.quote: From Middle Chinese compound 元氣 (MC ngjwon khj+jH, literally “first, fundamental, source + vapor, spirit, energy”). In Chinese cosmology, this represented the fundamental force that permeates all matter and life. Early Japanese borrowed this word and meaning. Later, this spelling was conflated with the meaning of homophone 減気 (genki, “recovery from illness”), adding in the modern senses related to healthy and wellness.

headline: A name is “name” plus “front” — and its look-alike in English is a coincidence.

sources.quote: Derived from 名 (na, “name”) + 前 (mae, front). Compare the semantics of Latin praenomen.
Appears as a term only in the last few centuries, becoming more widely used during the Meiji period.
Similarity to English name and other Indo-European words derived from Proto-Indo-European *h₁nómn̥ is coincidental.

headline: Banzai is a mixed reading: the second part kept an older Chinese sound while the first took a newer one.

sources.quote: Shift in reading from 万(ばん)歳(ぜい) (banzei) below, keeping the older goon reading for the second character and adopting the relatively newer kan'on reading for the first character. Doublet of マンセー (mansē).

headline: “Before” began as “what lies just in front of your hand”.

sources.quote: Compound of Old Japanese elements 手 (te, “hand”) + 前 (mae, “front”), originally meaning “that which is just in front of one's hand”.

headline: A rocket and a locket share one katakana spelling.

sources.quote: Borrowed from English rocket.
Borrowed from English locket.
